A B S T R A C T
The ‘‘Thoughts Management System’’ (TMS) is a novel framework that enables autonomous AI Agents to 
execute long-horizon tasks, inspired by the human mind’s ability to manage 60,000 thoughts per day. TMS 
empowers agents to dynamically prioritize goals, decompose complex objectives into actionable tasks, and 
adapt strategies over extended periods. TMS introduces a hierarchical goal decomposition mechanism for 
breaking down high-level tasks, combined with self-critique modules that iteratively evaluate progress and 
refine decision-making. By integrating reinforcement learning reward mechanisms, agents focus on high-value 
tasks while eliminating irrelevant ones, ensuring efficiency and goal alignment.
Built on our prior work, ‘‘LLMAgentNet: A Collaborative Network of Autonomous AI Agents,’’ TMS uses 
a multi-agent system (MAS) where specialized agents collaborate to achieve shared goals. Techniques like 
Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) balance exploration and exploitation for optimal performance in dynamic 
environments. By mimicking human thought management, TMS enables AI Agents to sustain focus, adapt 
dynamically, and self-improve over time. This framework marks a significant advancement toward autonomous 
AI systems capable of solving real-world, long-term challenges across domains such as marketing, scientific 
discovery, and infrastructure management.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.text: statement Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized Artificial Intel- ligence (AI), enabling the development of AI Agents. AI Agents are systems that utilize LLMs to autonomously perform tasks by interact- ing with tools and external systems. Current AI Agents are proficient at generating step-by-step plans, executing actions, reasoning about intermediate results, and adapting strategies based on user input or environmental feedback. This has led to the creation of digital workers capable of handling well-defined tasks efficiently. However, a critical limitation persists: AI Agents are not capable of sustaining long-term autonomy without continuous human input or predefined task boundaries. Current implementations execute fixed tasks explicitly provided by users and are unable to undertake long- horizon planning and decision-making. For truly autonomous agents, the goal is to: 1. Execute high-level, complex tasks autonomously over extended time periods (hours, days, or even months) 2. Continuously plan, adapt, and reason dynamically, refining goals and strategies as they interact with changing environments ∗ Corresponding author. E-mail addresses: andrii.r.bidochko@lpnu.ua (A. Incorporate self-critique and evaluation mechanisms to assess progress and adjust their execution, with human reviews serving as optional guidance The ultimate objective is to develop AI Agents that can autonomously receive high-level objectives, adapt to dynamic conditions, and work independently toward achieving those goals. Such agents would revo- lutionize automation and digital workforces, reducing human interven- tion and extending their operational horizons. 2.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: The rapid advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have en- abled the development of AI Agents capable of performing increasingly complex tasks [ 1 , 2 ]. However, current AI systems remain constrained by their inability to autonomously manage high-level goals and execute long-horizon tasks without continuous human intervention [ 3 , 4 ]. While humans naturally manage approximately 60,000 thoughts per day, pri- oritizing, switching, and focusing on the most relevant tasks, AI Agents lack this intrinsic ability to organize and refine their actions over https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jocs.2025.102740 Received 17 April 2025; Received in revised form 23 August 2025; Accepted 29 October 2025 Journal of Computational Science 93 (2026) 102740 Available online 6 November 2025 1877-7503/© 2025 Published by Elsevier B.V. A. Bidochko and Y. Vyklyuk extended time periods. This gap limits their capacity to handle dynamic environments and real-world problems requiring sustained effort [ 5 ]. Inspiration can be drawn from the human cognitive process of man- aging thoughts—a natural system where individuals filter, prioritize, and act upon tasks to achieve both immediate and long-term goals [ 6 , 7 ]. Humans navigate distractions, eliminate unproductive thoughts, and dynamically adapt strategies to remain focused and productive. Translating this process into AI systems is essential for building agents capable of reasoning, adapting, and improving performance over time. To address these challenges, we propose the Thoughts Management System (TMS), a framework that mirrors the human ability to manage thoughts. TMS enables AI Agents to break down high-level goals into actionable sub-goals, dynamically prioritize objectives, and continu- ously refine their strategies [ 8 ]. By leveraging reinforcement learning reward mechanisms, agents are encouraged to focus on high-value tasks while filtering out irrelevant or ‘‘bad’’ thoughts that fail to contribute to the overall goal [ 9 , 10 ]. Additionally, TMS builds upon our prior work, "LLMAgentNet’’, which introduced a collaborative network of autonomous AI Agents for complex task execution [ 11 ]. TMS expands on this concept by incorporating self-critique modules and structured search techniques, such as Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), to balance exploration and exploitation during task execution [ 12 , 13 ]. The proposed system offers a scalable and adaptable solution for enabling AI Agents to achieve autonomy in long-horizon tasks across diverse domains. Through dynamic reasoning, self-improvement, and multi-agent collaboration, the TMS framework opens new possibilities for AI-driven solutions in marketing, scientific discovery, infrastructure management, and beyond [ 14 , 15 ]. In the following sections, we will discuss the challenges associ- ated with long-horizon task execution, explain the TMS architecture in-depth, and evaluate its performance in real-world and simulated environments [ 16 – 18 ]. 3.

sections.heading: Review
sections.text: of recent research Existing LLM-based planning models. Several recent works, including SELFGOAL [ 18 ], ReAct [ 7 ], and SwiftSage [ 6 ], have explored the idea of LLM-driven autonomous planning. These models focus on prompt- based task structuring but lack a persistent, self-updating task tree. In contrast, TMS introduces a memory-augmented, recursive planning structure, where the Signal Generator continuously evaluates, scores, and expands the Tree of Thoughts (ToT) based on the system’s evolv- ing needs. This design enables continuous self-improvement without requiring manual interventions or external reinforcement. LLMs for decision-making and hierarchical planning. Language models have increasingly been used in decision-making tasks across multi- ple domains, including robotics [ 1 , 2 ], text-based environments [ 3 – 5 ], and social interactions [ 6 ]. However, traditional LLM-based decision- making models struggle with long-horizon, goal-driven reasoning, often failing to maintain task consistency over extended interactions [ 7 , 8 ]. Several approaches have been proposed to enhance planning capabil- ities in LLMs, such as hierarchical decomposition [ 4 ], structured goal representations [ 5 ], and reinforcement learning-based adaptations [ 9 ]. Unlike these approaches, TMS does not require fine-tuning or param- eter updates for LLMs; instead, it structures its reasoning using a Tree of Thoughts (ToT), enabling self-directed, iterative planning. Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (HRL) and task decomposition. Hi- erarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) has been widely explored as a method to decompose complex problems into manageable subgoals [ 14 , 15 ]. Techniques such as option-based reinforcement learning [ 14 ] and temporal abstraction in hierarchical task networks (HTN) [ 15 ] have shown that structured goal decomposition improves AI planning ca- pabilities. In the context of TMS, the hierarchical nature of the Tree of Thoughts (ToT) allows dynamic goal generation and task execu- tion without explicit reinforcement learning updates. This modular- ity makes TMS more flexible than traditional HRL approaches, as it adapts to long-horizon tasks without relying on predefined state–action mappings. For instance, frameworks like SELFGOAL [ 18 ] utilize an adaptive hierarchical structure (e.g., a GOALTREE) to refine tasks dynamically based on real-time feedback. These systems enable agents to prioritize subgoals and adapt strategies, demonstrating improved performance in tasks requiring long-horizon planning and delayed rewards. However, SELFGOAL relies on fixed modules, such as Search, Decomposition, and Act, which may limit flexibility when handling dynamic multi-agent environments. Building on these advancements, the Thought Management System (TMS) introduces the Tree of Thoughts (ToT), a modular and memory- augmented structure designed for autonomous reasoning and task re- finement. Unlike static frameworks, TMS employs a Signal Generator to evaluate the tree state iteratively, ensuring tasks are dynamically aligned with system capabilities and environmental constraints. Multi-agent coordination and execution in AI systems. Recent research has explored multi-agent systems (MAS) for task execution, particularly in cooperative AI environments [ 16 ]. Systems like TravelPlanner [ 11 ] and Voyager [ 8 ] leverage multiple AI agents to perform collaborative task solving. However, many of these models operate with static task assignments or predefined execution logic. TMS integrates MAS capa- bilities dynamically, ensuring that Execution Requests (ERs) are only generated when feasible based on available agents and tools. This real- time capability alignment differentiates TMS from existing multi-agent task planning approaches. Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) in planning systems. This structure enables agents to iteratively refine their goals, dynamically adapt to feedback, and maintain focus on long-term objectives. Unlike traditional methods that rely on static workflows, TMS leverages dynamic components that facilitate exploration, evaluation, and refinement in real-time. To achieve fully autonomous AI Agents capable of executing long- horizon tasks, we propose a novel framework for Long-Horizon Au- tonomous AI Agents that integrates adaptive goal decomposition, search mechanisms, and self-critique feedback loops. This framework is struc- tured to facilitate long-term, autonomous execution of high-level tasks by a coordinated team of specialized AI Agents. Key innovations in TMS include 1. Hierarchical Goal Decomposition: Decomposes high-level tasks into intermediate goals and sub-tasks using a dynamic, hierar- chical approach. This module iteratively updates the sub-goal tree (GOALTREE) as agents interact with the environment and receive feedback. 2. Adaptive Planning Module: Enables real-time refinement of task plans based on progress tracking and changing conditions. 3. Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) for Exploration: Employs MCTS to explore the action space and identify optimal paths toward task completion. The search is guided by heuristic rewards based on intermediate results. 4. Self-Critique Mechanism: Introduces an AI-driven feedback loop to evaluate search outcomes, providing refined rewards for ac- tion steps and improving the decision-making process. 5. Self-Evaluation and Learning: Agents incorporate Direct Prefer- ence Optimization (DPO) to learn from both successful and failed trajectories, ensuring continual improvement. The system tracks task progress, identifies bottlenecks, and dynamically reallocates resources to underperforming areas. 4.1. Functional modules of Thoughts Management System The Thoughts Management System (TMS) is built upon four interde- pendent modules, each serving a unique role in enabling autonomous agents to manage and execute long-horizon tasks effectively. Together, these modules form the foundation of the Tree of Thoughts framework, facilitating dynamic goal decomposition, execution planning, and eval- uation. Each module operates as an independent agent powered by Large Language Models (LLMs), collaborating to extend the Tree of Thoughts and simulate a human-like thought process.

sections.heading: Generator
sections.text: The Signal Generator is the core decision- making unit of TMS. It is an LLM Agent responsible for evaluating the current state of the Tree of Thoughts (ToT), assigning a score (0–100), and selecting one of the four available expansion options. The reasoning behind the decision is also generated as part of the process. Based on its evaluation, the Signal Generator chooses exactly one option per iteration. Once an option is selected, the corresponding module (Thoughts Generator, Executions Generator, or Thoughts Exploitation) is activated. Key Responsibilities: • Evaluate the current state of the tree and assign a score • Select the most appropriate expansion option based on system heuristics • Provide explanations for the selected action to ensure trans- parency • Trigger the corresponding module (Thoughts Generator, Execu- tions Generator, or Thoughts Exploitation) This decision-making mechanism ensures that the system follows a structured and rational approach to problem-solving. The Signal Generator’s role is illustrated in Fig. 2 , showing its central position in the workflow.

sections.heading: Generator
sections.text: The Thoughts Generator is an LLM Agent responsible for generating high-level goals and subgoals. It is activated when the Signal Generator selects either Option 1 or Option 2: Option 1 (New Goal) creates a new high-level Goal under the ROOT. For example, if the ROOT is ‘‘Expand user engagement’’, a new Goal could be ’’Develop a content marketing strategy’’. Option 2 (New Subgoal) decomposes a Goal into practical Subgoals. For example, if the Goal is ‘‘Develop a content marketing strategy’’, a Subgoal could be ’’Create weekly blog posts’’.

sections.heading: Generator
sections.text: The Executions Generator handles the creation of Execution Requests (ERs) for Subgoals. It is triggered when the Signal Generator selects Option 3. Option 3 (New Execution Request) — converts a Subgoal into an executable task that can be processed by the Multi-Agent System (MAS). For example, if the Subgoal is ‘‘Create weekly blog posts’’, an Execution Request could be ’’Generate blog post draft using AI writer’’. Execution management then ensures that the generated ER is trans- mitted to the MAS for execution. The MAS completes the task and returns results, which are subsequently passed on for validation.

sections.heading: Exploitation
sections.text: The Thoughts Exploitation Module is triggered when the Signal Generator selects Option 4, which is a special case focused on deepening reasoning and refining completed tasks. Precondition: The selected Subgoal must have at least one fulfilled Execution Request. Option 4 (Subgoal Refinement Process) generates a new Subgoal based on three factors: (1) the selected Subgoal, (2) the fulfilled Execu- tion Requests, and (3) the current capabilities of the MAS. For example, if the Subgoal is ‘‘Design Instagram ads’’ and the fulfilled Execution Request is "Generate ad copy’’, the new Subgoal could be "Analyze ad performance data’’. Iterative refinement allows this process to be repeated multiple times, enabling the system to continuously expand and adapt tasks in high-value directions. sections.heading: Validator
sections.text: The Validator Module ensures that execution results are correct, useful, and well-documented. It is responsible for analyzing results returned by the MAS. Its operation follows three main steps: • Validate execution results — the system checks whether the com- pleted task matches the expected outcome. • Generate explanation — a reasoning step is performed to justify the validation decision. • Summarize outputs — execution results are condensed and stored for future reference. For example, if an Execution Request was "Generate blog post draft using AI writer’’, the Validator examines whether a draft has been produced, whether it complies with content guidelines, and whether further revisions are necessary. These five modules, functioning as independent agents on top of LLMs, work in unison to create a scalable and adaptive framework that dynamically adjusts to the needs of long-horizon tasks. The Thoughts Generator lays the groundwork, the Execution Request Generator oper- ationalizes the plans, the Thoughts Exploitation Module ensures adapt- ability, and the Validator Module maintains quality control. Together, they empower TMS to achieve robust, autonomous decision-making across diverse domains, mimicking the collaborative and iterative na- ture of human thought processes. sections.heading: Node
sections.text: The Root node serves as the anchor for the Tree of Thoughts and represents the primary high-level goal of the system. It acts as the ‘‘north star’’ guiding all subsequent reasoning and actions. The Root node is the parent to all Goal nodes, establishing the top-level structure of the tree, and contains a concise description of the main goal.

sections.heading: Nodes
sections.text: Execution Requests represent the most concrete tasks within the ToT, designed to be executed by the Multi-Agent System. They translate Subgoals into actionable tasks for execution. ER Nodes have two states: • Pending: Awaiting execution • Fulfilled: Completed with results and execution logs 4.3. Algorithm powering the Thought Management System The Thoughts Management System (TMS) operates using a struc- tured algorithm designed to dynamically expand and refine a Tree of Thoughts (ToT). The process starts by initializing the Tree of Thoughts, which forms the hierarchical backbone for the reasoning and task management within TMS. Starting from ROOT: The simplest initialization begins with a single ROOT node, which represents the primary high-level goal or objective (e.g., ‘‘Increase Monthly Active Users (MAU) from 1,000 to 3,000’’). Predefined Tree: Alternatively, TMS can initialize using a predefined ToT with multiple nodes, including goals, subgoals, and execution requests. This approach allows users to save the state of a ToT at any point and later resume execution from that state. These predefined trees act as memories for the TMS, capturing previous trajectories and enabling more efficient future reasoning. By supporting both initialization modes, TMS ensures flexibility for a wide range of applications, whether starting from scratch or resuming a paused workflow. At each iteration, the Signal Generator determines how to expand the tree by analyzing its current state and aligning with available agent capabilities. This decision-making process is iterative and adapts dynamically to the environment: 1. Create a new Goal for the ROOT: Expands the tree by adding a high-level Goal node connected to the ROOT 2. Create a new Subgoal for a selected Goal: Adds a practical Subgoal node as a child of an existing Goal node 3. Create a new Execution Request for a selected Subgoal: Gener- ates an actionable Execution Request as a child of a Subgoal node 4. Create a new Subgoal for a Subgoal with fulfilled Execution Requests: Enables deeper refinement by adding a new Subgoal under a completed Subgoal with at least one fulfilled Execution Request The step-by-step process of TMS is detailed in Algorithm 1 , which outlines how the Signal Generator interacts with the ToT, evaluates its Journal of Computational Science 93 (2026) 102740 5 A. At every iteration, the system ensures that the tasks generated are aligned with the capabilities of the MAS and actionable in the given context.

sections.text: the final Tree of Thoughts 𝑇 The performance of TMS can be quantified using several key met- rics: Task Completion Rate = Number of Successfully Completed Tasks Total Number of Tasks × 100% (4) Execution Efficiency = Total Execution Time Number of Tasks (seconds/task) (5) Resource Utilization = Active Agent Time Total Available Time × 100% (6) These metrics provide a quantitative basis for evaluating TMS’s per- formance in managing and executing tasks within the MAS framework. A key advantage of TMS is its ability to exploit past execution results (Option 4), allowing the system to refine and optimize decision-making over time. This iterative exploitation ensures that high-value pathways are continuously explored, leading to progressively better outcomes in complex, real-world tasks. The system’s integration with MAS capabilities ensures that all generated tasks are feasible and executable, preventing wasted effort on tasks that agents cannot complete. Additionally, TMS supports both fresh problem-solving and resuming from memory, enabling continuity in long-term projects. In conclusion, the Thought Management System (TMS) represents a powerful and adaptive approach to AI-driven task management. By systematically breaking down goals into structured tasks, leveraging execution feedback, and optimizing decision-making, TMS provides a scalable and intelligent framework for achieving complex objectives efficiently.

sections.heading: Management
sections.text: Humans naturally switch between tasks throughout the day, managing a con- stant influx of thoughts and prioritizing goals to maintain productivity. Our proposed Thoughts Management System mirrors this process in AI Agents: • Cognitive Load Management: AI Agents distribute workloads across tasks, ensuring focus on the most critical objectives without overwhelming resources • Dynamic Task Switching: Agents, like humans, can seamlessly shift focus between tasks, revisit unfinished goals, and adapt to new priorities as they arise • Goal Tracking and Reflection: Inspired by human introspection, agents continuously monitor progress toward goals, adjust strate- gies, and reflect on their performance to improve efficiency 4.4. Embedding TMS into Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) The Thought Management System (TMS) serves as an advanced task generation and coordination engine for Multi-Agent Systems (MAS), en- suring continuous operation without requiring direct human interven- tion. Unlike traditional MAS setups that rely on human input to initiate tasks, TMS autonomously generates Execution Requests, dynamically adapting based on system feedback and evolving requirements. Fig. 4 demonstrates how TMS seamlessly integrates with MAS, or- chestrating the interaction between Agent Hubs, Multi-Agent Systems, and external execution tools.

sections.heading: Systems
sections.text: Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) are often designed to execute predefined tasks or re- spond to human instructions. While this approach works in limited, task-specific scenarios, it creates several challenges when MAS is ex- pected to replace entire departments or individual employees: 1. Dependence on Human Input: MAS systems typically remain idle until provided with explicit instructions from a user. This ‘‘wait- ing state’’ limits their ability to act proactively or autonomously, reducing their overall utility and efficiency 2. Human Bottlenecks: When humans must constantly generate tasks for MAS, the system’s scalability is constrained by hu- man availability and capacity. This reliance also introduces de- lays and inefficiencies, particularly in high-demand, fast-paced environments 3. Underutilization of MAS Capabilities: Without continuous task generation, MAS systems fail to fully leverage their capabilities, often operating below their potential A

sections.heading: Integration
sections.text: One of the key advantages of TMS is its ability to integrate with any MAS, re- gardless of the underlying framework. The system architecture enables communication between TMS and MAS via REST API (HTTP), making it highly flexible, modular, and scalable. This framework-agnostic ap- proach ensures that TMS can work with various MAS implementations, including those built on: • LangChain • UBOS • CrewAI • LlamaIndex • LLMAgentNet This compatibility allows organizations to enhance existing MAS setups without requiring major modifications, simply by connecting TMS via its standardized API.

Task Generation: TMS replaces the need for human-generated input by autonomously generating tasks that align with the north star goal defined by the user. Once initialized with a high-level objective, TMS continuously works to: • Break down the primary goal into smaller, actionable tasks • Prioritize and schedule these tasks for execution by MAS • Adaptively refine tasks based on execution outcomes 2. Self-Evolution Through Feedback: TMS monitors the execution results of tasks completed by MAS. This feedback loop allows TMS to: • Assess task outcomes for quality and efficiency • Learn from successful and failed executions to improve future task generation • Continuously refine its task generation strategies based on evolving MAS capabilities

sections.heading: TMS
sections.text: In traditional systems, humans serve as intermediaries, defining tasks for MAS to execute. However, this approach introduces inefficiencies and limits scalability. By replacing the human-in-the-loop with TMS, organizations can: • Achieve Autonomy: TMS ensures MAS systems remain productive without requiring constant human intervention • Unlock Scalability: With TMS managing task generation, MAS systems can handle larger workloads without being constrained by human availability • Improve Consistency: TMS provides a consistent flow of tasks tailored to MAS capabilities, reducing errors and variability in- troduced by human-generated inputs

sections.heading: MAS
sections.text: During extensive testing across various MAS implementations, TMS demonstrated its ability to: • Maintain Continuous Operation: Unlike traditional MAS systems that ‘‘sleep’’ in the absence of human instructions, TMS ensures uninterrupted task execution by continuously generating action- able tasks • Reduce Human Effort: By taking over the role of task genera- tion, TMS significantly reduces the time and effort required from human operators • Adapt to Evolving Objectives: As TMS learns from task out- comes and MAS capabilities, it evolves to generate increasingly sophisticated and effective instructions over time For example, in a simulated marketing department, TMS autonomously generated content creation, analytics, and strategy tasks for an MAS. The MAS executed these tasks, and TMS refined subsequent tasks based on execution results. This closed-loop system not only achieved the department’s goals but also outperformed human-led task management in terms of speed and efficiency. The integration of Thought Management Systems into Multi-Agent Systems transforms them into proactive, self-sustaining entities capable of continuous operation without human oversight. This advancement not only enhances efficiency and scalability but also opens new avenues for the application of autonomous systems across various industries. 5.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: and discussion The experimental setup aims to evaluate the effectiveness of the Thought Management System (TMS) in autonomously managing task generation and execution within Multi-Agent Systems (MAS). To ana- lyze the decision-making and expansion processes of TMS, we introduce a graph visualization and exploration tool, which provides a real-time representation of the Tree of Thoughts (ToT). This visualization enables a structured understanding of how TMS dynamically expands thoughts, generates goals, and orchestrates execution requests within MAS. In addition to visualizing the thought expansion process, we apply TMS in a real-world use case within the marketing industry. This implementation demonstrates how TMS can autonomously manage content generation, social media strategy, and campaign optimization, replacing traditional human-driven workflows with an AI-powered task management system. Through this case study, we assess TMS’s ability to operate as a self-evolving decision-making engine that continuously generates, refines, and executes tasks to achieve predefined business objectives. Vyklyuk In the following sections, we present the graph-based visualization framework, describe its role in analyzing TMS’s reasoning strategies, and introduce the marketing industry use case as a practical demon- stration of TMS’s ability to enhance real-world MAS-driven automation. This structured experimental setup ensures a comprehensive evaluation of TMS across both theoretical and applied domains, validating its role as a scalable, autonomous task management system. To evaluate the effectiveness of the Thought Management System (TMS) in autonomously managing Multi-Agent Systems (MAS), we designed a structured experimental setup to analyze its performance across different real-world and simulated environments. Our goal is to assess: • Task Generation Efficiency — How well TMS generates and re- fines tasks compared to human-driven workflows. • MAS Utilization and Execution Performance — Whether TMS effectively distributes tasks across agents and minimizes idle time. • Scalability and Adaptability — How TMS adapts to different MAS frameworks and dynamic execution environments. Our experiments were conducted using a variety of MAS implemen- tations, incorporating multiple agent types, APIs, and execution tools. The experimental framework evaluates TMS’s role as a self-sustaining decision-making module, eliminating the need for human-in-the-loop intervention. 5.1. Graph-based visualization of TMS Understanding the expansion and reasoning process of the Thought Management System (TMS) requires a structured representation of how it generates and refines tasks over time. To achieve this, we developed a graph-based visualization tool that provides a dynamic, real-time view of the Tree of Thoughts (ToT). This tool enables a deeper analysis of how TMS constructs goals, subgoals, and execution requests (ERs), allowing for a more intuitive understanding of TMS-driven task decomposition. Fig. 5 presents a labeled breakdown of the core node types in the visualization. The ROOT node, depicted as the largest and most central element, represents the primary goal of the system. From this starting point, TMS expands the tree by generating GOAL nodes, which correspond to major sub-objectives needed to achieve the main goal. Further task decomposition occurs through the creation of SubGoal nodes, which serve as intermediate steps between high-level objectives and executable tasks. The smallest nodes in the graph correspond to Execution Requests (ERs), representing actionable tasks sent to the Multi-Agent System (MAS) for processing. The graph not only illustrates the hierarchical relationship be- tween these nodes but also dynamically updates as TMS makes de- cisions. sections.text: These environments simulate household or office tasks requiring 10–20 sequential steps (e.g., ‘‘pick up the knife, wash it in the sink, and place it in the drawer’’). Success requires correct execution of all sub-steps, with observations provided at each action. 2.

sections.heading: Navigation
sections.text: (WebShop): Agents must fulfill a user request (e.g., ‘‘Find waterproof hiking boots under $80 with 4+ star reviews’’). The task requires searching, filtering, brows- ing, and decision-making under constraints. Success is defined by correctly satisfying the specified request. Both benchmarks allow precise logging of intermediate steps, mak- ing them ideal for assessing TMS’s ability to plan, decompose goals, and refine decisions over long horizons.

sections.heading: Setup
sections.text: TMS was deployed as the orchestration layer on top of GPT-4o and integrated with the environments. A ROOT goal was provided for each scenario (e.g., ‘‘Prepare the kitchen for cooking’’ or ‘‘Find waterproof hiking boots’’). The Signal Generator expanded goals into subgoals, the Execution Request Generator produced executable steps, the Thoughts Exploitation Module refined subgoals, and the Validator ensured correctness and prevented redundant actions.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: The experiments confirm that TMS achieves: 1. Higher task success compared to CoT, ReAct, and ToT. 2. Greater efficiency, completing tasks in fewer steps. 3. More stable decision trajectories with reduced backtracking. These results demonstrate TMS’s strength as a scalable orchestra- tion framework for long-horizon reasoning. By adaptively combining breadth-first exploration and depth-first refinement, TMS aligns with the dynamic demands of embodied and web-based environments. 5.7. Real-world application: Marketing department simulation To validate the effectiveness of the Thought Management System (TMS) in a real-world setting, we simulate its integration within a Marketing Department tasked with increasing monthly website visi- tors from 500 to 2,000 users. In this scenario, TMS acts as an au- tonomous coordinator, orchestrating tasks across a Multi-Agent System (MAS) composed of specialized agents, ensuring continuous execution, adaptive goal refinement, and strategic optimization. TMS decomposes high-level marketing objectives into structured sub-tasks – Content Creation, SEO Optimization, Social Media Market- ing, and Analytics – ensuring alignment with overall goals. It dynami- cally expands the Tree of Thoughts (ToT), structuring execution so that each task contributes to the primary objective. AI agents, specialized in distinct workflow components, operate autonomously under TMS, optimizing execution in real time. Acting as central intelligence, TMS coordinates tasks, resolves dependencies, and tracks performance, minimizing human oversight. Unlike static workflows, TMS adapts dynamically using multi-step evaluation and self-critique: • Reallocates resources to high-performing tasks (e.g., shifting bud- gets from low-performing ads to high-engagement content) • Uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to explore optimal strate- gies • Continuously refines decision-making through self-evaluation Integrated with MAS, TMS autonomously executes marketing strate- gies, measures impact, and iterates toward the 2,000-user goal with minimal human input. Real-time tracking ensures adaptability to mar- ket trends, campaign performance, and MAS feedback. Unlike conven- tional workflows, TMS-driven marketing is: • Fully autonomous after goal definition • Continuously evolving, dynamically adjusting strategies • Optimized for efficiency through resource reallocation To assess the impact of integrating TMS with MAS, we compare our new approach (TMS + MAS) with our previous MAS-only content marketing system (LLMAgentNet). The goal is to determine how much efficiency, automation, and cost-effectiveness improve when shifting from a user-driven MAS workflow to a fully autonomous TMS-driven MAS workflow. sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we introduced the Thought Management System (TMS), a novel framework designed to enable long-horizon, goal-driven reasoning in Large Language Model (LLM)-powered agents. Inspired by the human cognitive process of thought management, TMS structures autonomous decision-making into a hierarchical framework known as the Tree of Thoughts (ToT). This framework enables AI Agents to con- tinuously generate, refine, and execute tasks in dynamic environments without requiring human intervention. Unlike traditional Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) that remain idle with- out explicit user instructions, TMS autonomously orchestrates the exe- cution flow, transforming static agent architectures into self-sustaining, goal-driven entities. By introducing hierarchical goal decomposition, multi-agent collaboration, and iterative self-improvement mechanisms, TMS enables agents to dynamically explore problem spaces, optimize execution strategies, and evolve their decision-making processes over time. Our experiments demonstrate that TMS significantly enhances MAS execution efficiency, enabling a 24/7 autonomous workflow. Through graph-based visualizations, we analyzed the different expansion strate- gies employed by TMS – depth-first refinement and breadth-first exploration – which illustrate its ability to adaptively optimize task execution. Additionally, the integration of TMS into a real-world mar- keting workflow showcased substantial cost reductions and opera- tional improvements compared to traditional MAS-only systems. By autonomously generating content strategies, executing multi-step cam- paigns, and optimizing ad budgets, TMS outperformed human-driven content workflows in terms of scalability, consistency, and efficiency. Furthermore, TMS is a framework-agnostic solution, capable of inte- grating with various MAS architectures via REST API communication. This allows organizations to adopt TMS without modifying their ex- isting MAS frameworks, ensuring seamless deployment and scalability across different domains. Our findings suggest that TMS is a transformative step toward fully autonomous AI task management, shifting the role of LLM-based agents from reactive executors to proactive decision-makers. By removing the human bottleneck, TMS enables AI agents to function as self-evolving digital minds, continuously striving toward complex objectives without requiring constant user input. This advancement has broad implications for AI-powered workflow automation, business process optimization, and intelligent decision-making. Journal of Computational Science 93 (2026) 102740 15 A. Future work While TMS has demonstrated strong performance in autonomous task generation and execution, future research should explore its adapt- ability to more complex, multi-domain environments. Potential areas of improvement include: • Enhanced Reinforcement Learning Integration: Further optimiz- ing decision-making through reinforcement learning-based heuris- tics to improve long-term planning • Expanding Multi-Agent Collaboration: Enabling deeper coordina- tion between AI agents, allowing for more sophisticated execution of interdependent tasks • Memory-Augmented Reasoning: Improving the system’s ability to recall and utilize past execution data, enabling it to develop more strategic and long-term adaptive behaviors • Real-Time Human–AI Collaboration: Investigating hybrid work- flows, where TMS collaborates with human operators, allowing for more interactive and flexible decision-making With TMS paving the way for fully autonomous AI-driven task or- chestration, we envision a future where AI agents continuously operate, adapt, and improve, reshaping industries that rely on high-volume, knowledge-driven automation.
